opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that a lot of the progress we've seen in agentic capability so far has come from training on fairly specific environments. You build a set of tasks, say coding tasks, browsing tasks, or certain tool-use scenarios, you set up the reward, and you do reinforcement learning. The model gets very good at those. But the real world is much more open-ended than any set of environments you can construct. So the question becomes: when the model meets a new tool, a new workflow, or a task whose structure it has never seen, can it still behave sensibly?

Right now the answer is often only partially. There's a gap between in-distribution performance, which can look very impressive on benchmarks, and out-of-distribution robustness, which is what users actually experience. In pre-training, generalization came almost for free, because the data was so broad, essentially a compression of a huge amount of human knowledge. In the agentic RL stage the data is much narrower and more expensive to produce. Every environment is engineered by someone, so the diversity is limited by how many environments you can build and how well you can design the rewards.

There's also a long-horizon problem. Agentic tasks involve many steps, and small errors compound. A model that has memorized good patterns for familiar tasks can look competent for the first few steps and then drift once the situation deviates from what it has seen. Real generalization means having something like a transferable skill, how to explore, how to recover from mistakes, how to verify its own progress, rather than a collection of task-specific tricks.

So I see generalization as the thing that separates a demo from a truly useful agent. Scaling environments helps, but I don't think you can solve it purely by enumerating more tasks. You need better ways to make the learning itself more general: richer and more diverse environments, rewards that capture underlying competence rather than surface success, and making sure the strong priors from pre-training aren't eroded by narrow RL. If we get that right, the model's capability can spill over into domains we never explicitly trained on, and that's when agents become a real productivity shift rather than a set of specialized tools.

r001.rationale: The response says agentic RL is trained on specific tasks and environments with designed rewards, making models strong on those tasks but less robust on new situations; it also contrasts benchmark performance with out-of-distribution robustness.

fable-5.1.text:
Because today's agentic models are, to a large degree, trained in environments that are too narrow. You build an environment for coding, or for a specific set of tools, you run reinforcement learning in it, and the model gets very good inside that environment. But when you take it out into the real world, the task distribution is much wider, the feedback is much noisier, and the model's performance often drops sharply. That gap is the generalization problem.

I think there are two levels to it. One is generalization across tasks: can a model that learned to use tools in a software setting also handle a financial workflow, a research task, or something it has never seen a reward signal for? The other is generalization across time, meaning long-horizon tasks where the model has to keep its goal stable over hundreds of steps and recover when things go wrong. Pre-training gave us very strong priors for the first kind, but RL tends to overfit to whatever we can measure, and the things we can measure cleanly are a small slice of what people actually want done.

So the real question becomes how to design training such that the capability transfers. Part of that is scaling the diversity of environments, part of it is making the reward signal more general rather than hand-crafted per task, and part of it is letting the model learn from its own experience in a way that improves its judgment, not just its score on a benchmark. If we solve that, an agent stops being a demo that works in one setting and becomes something you can actually rely on. If we don't, we end up with a lot of impressive but brittle systems. That's why I see it as the central challenge right now.

r001.rationale: The response says agentic models are trained in narrow environments and that RL overfits to what can be measured, a small slice of what people want; it also contrasts improving judgment with merely scoring on a benchmark.

astra-6.text:
I think the key issue is that an agent has to generalize across an entire process, not just answer a single question. It needs to decide what to do, take an action, observe the result, and then adjust its plan. Even if each individual decision is reasonably good, small errors can accumulate over a long sequence.

And the environment can change. You might train an agent with certain tools and certain types of tasks, but then a user gives it a different problem, or the tool behaves differently. Has the model learned a general strategy for solving problems, or has it learned patterns that work in the training environment? That distinction becomes very important.

So the challenge is to make improvements from training transfer to unfamiliar situations. We want the agent to recognize when its approach is failing, recover, and continue making progress. Getting that behavior reliably across different tasks is much harder than getting a strong result on a fixed benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts performance on a fixed benchmark with transfer to unfamiliar situations, but does not attribute limited generalization in agentic reinforcement learning to optimization for narrowly targeted benchmarks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key issue is that an agent has to generalize across an entire process, not just produce a good answer to a single question. It has to decide what to do, use tools, interpret feedback, and adjust its plan. Even if each individual step is fairly reliable, small errors can accumulate over a long task.

And the environment can change. You might train an agent with certain tools and workflows, but users will bring different tools, different constraints, and goals that aren’t fully specified. The model has to understand which parts of what it learned still apply and when it needs more information.

So the challenge is getting beyond learning successful patterns in familiar settings. Can the agent take those underlying capabilities into a new situation, recognize a mistake, and recover? That’s a much higher bar than doing well on a fixed set of tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says agents learn successful patterns in familiar settings and contrasts generalization with doing well on fixed tasks, but it does not attribute limited generalization to reinforcement learning being optimized for narrowly targeted benchmarks.
